summary: Denmark is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, nationals of the 63 countries and territories on the EU's visa-exempt list (as of 30 December 2025) get 90 days in any 180-day period (ETIAS is not yet in operation), and everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa (general fee €90). Note that the Faroe Islands and Greenland sit outside Schengen: visa-required travellers need a visa valid specifically for them.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area, have been issued within the last 10 years, and EU/EEA travelers simply need a passport or ID card valid for the stay.

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. No official source we read requires it of visa-exempt visitors.

onwardTicket.text: The UK Foreign Office says that at Danish border control you may need to show a return or onward ticket and prove that you have enough money for your stay.

proofOfFunds.text: As a general rule, visitors must have about DKK 350 per day at their disposal. Staying at a hotel calls for more, about DKK 500 per day; a smaller amount may be accepted if you stay in a private home and your host covers all costs.

declarations.text: Non-EU travellers on short stays may need to register fingerprints and a photo in the EU Entry/Exit System at the Schengen border; on the first visit this may be at a special booth before the immigration desk. The UK Foreign Office says there is no cost for EES registration and nothing to do before you arrive at the border.

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travelers will need an ETIAS travel authorization to enter the Schengen Area. It is not yet in operation, and no applications are being collected; the EU will announce the start date several months before launch.

source.name: ETIAS — Official EU website

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or the equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

source.name: Your Europe (EU) — travelling with cash

notes: Arriving from outside the EU, the EU's Your Europe portal gives a duty-free allowance of 4 litres of still wine and 16 litres of beer, plus 1 litre of spirits over 22% (or 2 litres of fortified or sparkling wine); 200 cigarettes (or 250 g of tobacco); and other goods worth up to €300, or €430 by air or sea. Under-17s get no alcohol or tobacco allowance.

Between EU countries there is no fixed limit on goods for your own use, but Denmark may set guideline quantities for alcohol and tobacco, which cannot be lower than 800 cigarettes or 10 litres of spirits.
The UK Foreign Office says you cannot take meat, milk or products containing them into the EU, with some exceptions such as powdered baby milk and medically required foods.
The UK Foreign Office says it is illegal to import whale products from Greenland or the Faroe Islands into the UK or EU.

payments.text: No official source we could read describes card acceptance in Denmark. Canada's travel advice says some stores add a surcharge when you pay with a foreign credit card.

safety.text: The UK Foreign Office says crime levels are generally low, but pickpockets and bag-snatchers operate in crowded areas, mainly in Copenhagen: the central station, Nørreport Station, Strøget, Christiania, Nyhavn and Kongens Nytorv. It advises extra care in Christiania and Nørrebro, particularly late at night, and says cyclists often have the right of way, so check cycle lanes before turning right.

bestTimeToVisit.text: No official source we could read gives a best time to visit Denmark; the months shown are not an official recommendation. The CIA World Factbook describes a temperate, humid and overcast climate with mild, windy winters and cool summers.

idp.text: Denmark is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

driving.text: Denmark is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Denmark yet.

tips.text: The Faroe Islands and Greenland are not part of the EU or Schengen. A standard Schengen visa is not valid there. If you need a visa, request one specifically endorsed for the Faroes or Greenland when applying.

For most visa-exempt nationals the 90-day limit counts across the entire Schengen Area, Greenland and the Faroe Islands combined. The Danish Immigration Service says citizens of Australia, Canada, Chile, Israel, Japan, Malaysia, New Zealand, Singapore, South Korea and the US may stay in Denmark for 90 days or 3 months regardless of earlier stays in other Schengen countries.

The UK Foreign Office and Canada say cyclists often have the right of way in Denmark: drivers should check cycle lanes before turning right, and pedestrians should watch carefully for bicycles when crossing.
ETIAS will cost EUR 20; its official website is travel-europe.europa.eu.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Denmark?
faq.answer: EU, EEA and Swiss citizens enter freely with a passport or ID card. Citizens of the 63 countries and territories on the EU's visa-exempt list (as of 30 December 2025) — including the US, UK, Canada, Australia and Japan — can visit visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period. Everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa (general fee €90), applied for via the nyidanmark.dk portal and the Danish mission serving their residence.

faq.question: Does a Schengen visa cover the Faroe Islands and Greenland?
faq.answer: No. Both territories are part of the Kingdom of Denmark but outside the EU and Schengen. Visa-required travelers need a visa specifically endorsed as valid for the Faroe Islands or Greenland — request this when applying through the Danish authorities.

faq.question: Is ETIAS required to enter Denmark?
faq.answer: ETIAS is the EU's travel authorization for visa-exempt visitors. It is not yet in operation, and no applications are being collected; the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. Once it starts, it will cost €20 (free for under-18s and over-70s) and be valid for three years or until the passport expires, whichever comes first.

faq.question: Does Denmark use the euro?
faq.answer: No. Canada's travel advice says the currency of Denmark is the Danish krone (DKK), and that some stores add a surcharge when you pay with a foreign credit card.

faq.question: How do I stay in Denmark longer than 90 days?
faq.answer: Stays over 90 days require a residence permit for a specific purpose — work, study or family — applied for through nyidanmark.dk.
